Today's modern battle shows how an ancient monster collides with a familiar landmark.","enduringUnderstanding":"Authors choose specific words and figures of speech to create setting and tone. Heroes show courage by facing the unknown even when they feel unprepared.","futureLessons":"In Lesson 21 (Chapter 14), students will cite details of Percy's growing powers and analyze the fall and underwater sequence as a turning point. Today's work on how word choice shapes a scene prepares them to read that episode closely.","performanceTask":"In Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, students will cite descriptive language to explain how a scene is set up and how it blends old and new. Today's evidence-and-explanation practice builds that skill."},"vocabulary":[{"word":"confined","definition":"kept in a small space; limited or closed in","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"vicious","definition":"cruel, fierce, and dangerous","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"faithless","definition":"not loyal; not able to be trusted","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"plummeted","definition":"fell straight down very quickly","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"modernize","definition":"to update something old so it fits the present day","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"prowess","definition":"great skill or strength, especially in fighting","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"enraged","definition":"extremely angry","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"spectacle","definition":"an impressive, dramatic sight or public display","tier":"addressed"},{"word":"figurative language","definition":"words used in a creative, non-literal way, such as a comparison, to create an image or feeling","tier":"support"},{"word":"tone","definition":"the attitude or feeling an author's words create","tier":"support"},{"word":"trident","definition":"a three-pronged spear, the weapon linked to Poseidon","tier":"support"},{"word":"poisonous","definition":"containing a substance that can harm or kill","tier":"support"}],"texts":[{"title":"The Lightning Thief (Percy Jackson and the Olympians, Book 1), Chapter 13","author":"Rick Riordan","pages":"pp. 202-211"}]},"sections":[{"kind":"launch","title":"Launch","purpose":"Students activate prior knowledge of ancient myths and modern landmarks and predict how a classic monster battle might look in a familiar American place.","activities":[{"id":"launch-turn-and-talk","title":"Old Monster, New Place","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.1"],"routine":"Turn and Talk","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Turn and talk with your partner. Imagine an ancient Greek monster showing up at a famous place you know today, such as a mall, a stadium, or a giant landmark. Describe what would feel funny about it and what would feel frightening."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What would happen to a hero's courage if the monster showed up in a place that feels totally ordinary?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I think it would be harder because you wouldn't expect it. At a mall you feel safe, so a monster would be a bigger shock. It might also be kind of funny because monsters don't belong near a food court."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Today Percy faces an ancient monster at a famous American landmark, the Gateway Arch in St. Louis. Watch how Rick Riordan uses specific words to make that scene both funny and dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Keep this to 5 minutes. Take two or three quick shares and move on. The goal is to prime the idea of old meeting new, not to settle it."}]}]},{"kind":"literacy-lab","title":"Literacy Lab","purpose":"Students use context clues to determine the meanings of key words from Chapter 13, examine long i patterns and suffixes, and add the words to their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers.","activities":[{"id":"lab-context-clues","title":"Figuring Out Words from Context","minutes":6,"standards":["L.6.4.a","L.6.6"],"routine":"Introduce New Words Using Context Clues","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 13","pages":"pp. 202-211"},{"type":"directions","text":"Find each word in Chapter 13 as your teacher reads the sentence aloud. Underline clues in the sentence or the sentences around it that help you figure out what the word means. Then say your meaning to a partner."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Teach: *confined, vicious, faithless, plummeted*. For each word, read the sentence from the text, point out the context clue, and have students predict a meaning before you confirm it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A word's meaning is often hiding in its sentence. I look at the words around it, and I ask what job the word is doing. Is it describing a place, a creature, or an action? For *confined*, I look at where the characters are. If they are stuck in a tight, closed space, then *confined* must mean kept in a small space."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which clue in the sentence helps you figure out what *confined* means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The text describes a small, cramped space the characters are stuck in. That clue makes me think confined means kept inside a small place so you can't move around."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"The text calls the Chimera *vicious*. What does the description of its behavior tell you the word means?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Chimera attacks and spits fire and tries to hurt them. So vicious must mean mean, fierce, and dangerous."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"*Faithless* is used to describe a monster or enemy. Look at the suffix *-less*. What do you think *faithless* means, and which clue from the sentence confirms it?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"-less means without, so faithless means without faith or loyalty. The sentence is about someone who can't be trusted, which fits."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Percy and the others *plummeted*. What does the action in the scene tell you about this word?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"They fall from a really high place, and it happens fast. So plummeted means fell straight down quickly."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Please check the exact sentences in your copy of pp. 202-211 before class so you read the real context for each word. If a word's context is thinner than expected, add one clue from the surrounding paragraph. Quick definitions for the rest of the list: *modernize* (update an old thing for today), *prowess* (great skill in fighting), *enraged* (extremely angry), *spectacle* (a dramatic sight). Use them naturally in Part A, and students will meet them again in the organizer."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Using context to infer a word's meaning","tryThis":"Have students underline the clue and complete the frame: The clue ___ makes me think ___ means ___. Then have them act out or sketch the word (confined, plummeted) before writing a definition."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Using context to infer a word's meaning","tryThis":"Ask students to write a new sentence for vicious or enraged that contains a context clue strong enough that a partner could guess the meaning without the word being defined."}]}]},{"id":"lab-phonics-organizer","title":"Phonics and the Unit Vocabulary Organizer","minutes":4,"standards":["L.6.6"],"routine":"Word Study and Graphic Organizer","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Add all eight words to your Unit Vocabulary graphic organizer: confined, vicious, faithless, plummeted, modernize, prowess, enraged, spectacle. Record a definition in your own words and one clue from the text or a sentence of your own."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Look at *confined* and *trident*. Both have a long *i* sound, the vowel says its name. In *confined* the pattern is *i-n-e*, and in *trident* the *i* is in an open syllable, *tri-*. Say them with me."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Now look at the endings of *poisonous* and *faithless*. The suffix *-ous* means full of, so *poisonous* means full of poison. The suffix *-less* means without, so *faithless* means without faith. Suffixes can help you read a word and understand it."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Using the suffixes, what would *fearless* and *dangerous* mean?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Fearless means without fear, and dangerous means full of danger. The suffix tells me the idea."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"Circulate while students fill in the organizer. Make sure each entry has a definition in the student's own words, not a copied dictionary line."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in using word parts and context to build precise word meanings and in recording them in the organizer.","sayAsk":"Have students say each word aloud with a partner and tap the syllables. Ask: Which word part do you recognize? Frames: I think ___ means ___ because the clue ___ shows ___. The suffix -less means ___, so faithless means ___. Invite students to connect words to home-language cognates, for example Spanish *furioso* for enraged and *espectáculo* for spectacle.","watchFor":"If students copy a long definition without understanding it, then prompt: Say the meaning in your own words as if you were telling a younger student. If students ignore the suffix, then ask: What does -ous or -less tell you? Success looks like students using a clue from the sentence or word part to explain a meaning."}]}]},{"kind":"learning-in-action","title":"Learning in Action","purpose":"Part A: Students cite descriptive details to show how Riordan modernizes the hero-versus-monster battle. Part B: Students interpret figurative language and explain how word choice shapes tone. Part C: Students write an evidence-based explanation.","activities":[{"id":"lia-modern-battle-details","title":"Part A: Modernizing the Monster Battle","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.1","RL.6.6"],"routine":"Close Read and Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 13","pages":"pp. 202-211"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Teach: *Modernizing a classic battle.* In a classic myth, a hero faces a monster in a wild, ancient place. Riordan modernizes the battle by placing it somewhere familiar, using everyday comparisons, and having a narrator who sounds like a real kid."},{"type":"directions","text":"Reread pp. 202-211. Make a two-column chart. Column 1: Details about the Gateway Arch and its modern setting. Column 2: Details about the Chimera and how it fights. Add a third row labeled Old and New and note where an ancient idea meets a modern one. Use quotation marks for exact words and paraphrase everything else."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"I notice that the Arch is a real landmark that readers might have visited. When Riordan puts an ancient monster there, the modern place makes the monster feel more surprising and more real. I'll underline words that tell me what the place looks like, because those details help the reader picture a modern setting."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What details show you that this battle takes place in a modern setting?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The battle happens at the Gateway Arch in St. Louis, a real tourist spot. The text describes the Arch and the visitor areas, so it feels like a regular place people go. A monster showing up there makes the ancient story feel like it's happening today."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which descriptive details help you picture the Chimera, and how does it fight?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"The Chimera is a mix of animals, with a lion, a goat, and a snake tail. It breathes fire and the snake is poisonous, so it attacks in lots of ways at once. In the text it lunges at the heroes and they have to dodge it, which makes it sound vicious."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does Percy, the narrator, tell the battle? What does his way of telling it add to the modern feeling?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy tells it in first person like a regular kid. He makes jokes and compares scary things to everyday things. That makes the monster battle feel modern and personal, and I can tell how nervous he is."},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"note","text":"Accept any accurate details from pp. 202-211. Push students to move from naming a detail to explaining what it shows. Listen for verbs that describe battle mechanics (lunged, lashed, dodged, plummeted, spewed) and celebrate them. Use the simple present when explaining: The Chimera lunges at Percy, which shows it is vicious."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in reading closely and in explaining a scene using precise battle verbs in the correct tense.","sayAsk":"Model the present tense for literary analysis: Riordan describes the Arch as ___. The Chimera lunges, and Percy dodges. Frames: The setting shows ___ because ___. The author uses the word ___ to show ___. This detail makes the battle feel modern because ___. Let students rehearse with a partner first, using gestures for verbs like lunge, dodge, and plummet.","watchFor":"If students retell the plot in the past tense only, then prompt: When we explain what the author does, we use present tense. Try: Riordan shows... If students list details without linking them, then ask: What do these details tell you about the old and the new? Success looks like students citing a detail and explaining the effect with a present-tense verb."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Finding and explaining descriptive details","tryThis":"Give students a sentence frame: On page ___, the author describes ___, which shows ___. Have them point to one detail on the page first, then say it aloud before writing."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Finding and explaining descriptive details","tryThis":"Ask students to compare the Gateway Arch setting to the setting of a classic myth they know, such as a labyrinth or a cave, and explain what is gained by modernizing it."}]}]},{"id":"lia-figurative-language-tone","title":"Part B: Figurative Language and Tone","minutes":12,"standards":["RL.6.4","L.6.4.a","RL.6.1"],"routine":"Think-Pair-Share","blocks":[{"type":"text-reference","title":"The Lightning Thief, Chapter 13","pages":"pp. 202-211"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"teach","text":"Teach: *Figurative language and tone.* Figurative language uses words in a creative, non-literal way. The author's word choice shapes tone, the feeling that comes through. Riordan mixes humor and danger, so the same scene makes us laugh and worry."},{"type":"directions","text":"Find the place where Percy calls the Arch a \"huge shopping bag handle.\" Reread the paragraph. Think about the literal meaning and the figurative meaning. Then think, pair, and share: Why does Percy use this comparison, and what tone does it create?"},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"A *shopping bag handle* is something small, ordinary, and a little silly. The Arch is huge and famous. When Percy compares the two, the comparison makes the landmark feel everyday and funny, but the word *huge* reminds us how high up and dangerous it is."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does the phrase \"huge shopping bag handle\" show about how Percy sees the Arch?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It shows Percy sees the Arch as an ordinary thing, like something from a store, not a grand monument. It sounds like a regular kid thinking of everyday objects, so it's funny."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"How does this word choice affect the tone of the scene? Is it only funny?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"It makes the tone humorous because the comparison is silly. But the word huge also shows how high the Arch is, so there's still danger. The tone is funny and tense at the same time."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Find one more word or phrase in the chapter that adds humor or tension. What do you think it means, and how did you figure it out?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"I picked a phrase where Percy describes the monster in a sarcastic way. I used the sentence around it to figure out he is making a joke, but the monster is still really dangerous. The word choice shows he is scared but covers it with humor."},{"type":"pulse-check","standards":["RL.6.4"],"stem":"Why does Percy call the Gateway Arch a \"huge shopping bag handle\"?","choices":[{"text":"To show that he thinks the Arch is boring and not worth visiting","correct":false,"rationale":"This confuses humor with a boring attitude. Percy's comparison is a joke that uses everyday language, not a statement that the Arch is dull."},{"text":"To compare the famous landmark to an ordinary object, which adds humor while still showing how big and high it is","correct":true,"rationale":"The comparison makes the Arch feel ordinary and funny, and the word huge keeps the sense of height and danger, so the tone is both humorous and high-stakes."},{"text":"To prove that the Arch is made of the same material as a shopping bag","correct":false,"rationale":"This takes the phrase literally. It is figurative language, a comparison about shape and feeling, not material."},{"text":"To warn the reader that the Arch is about to fall down","correct":false,"rationale":"Nothing in the comparison predicts the Arch collapsing. The phrase shapes tone and helps readers picture the Arch."}]},{"type":"teacher-note","variant":"tip","text":"If students say the tone is only funny, point back to words like huge, plummeted, and vicious, and ask what feeling those words create. Aim for the idea that humor and danger coexist."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in evaluating how an author's language choices create tone and in using precise verbs to explain their thinking.","sayAsk":"Say: Authors choose words on purpose. Ask: Which word surprised you? Frames: Riordan compares ___ to ___, which makes the tone ___. The phrase ___ suggests ___. This word choice shows that Percy feels ___. Allow Emerging students to point to the phrase and complete a one-sentence frame; Bridging students can add the connector which shows that.","watchFor":"If students explain the phrase literally, then ask: Is the Arch really a shopping bag handle? What is the author comparing? If students name the tone with only one word, then prompt: Is there another feeling in the same scene? Success looks like students naming both humor and tension and linking each to a specific word."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Interpreting figurative language","tryThis":"Have students draw the literal picture and the real picture side by side, then complete: The author compares ___ to ___ to show ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Interpreting figurative language","tryThis":"Ask students to rewrite the sentence in a serious, formal tone and compare how the meaning and mood change. Have them explain what Riordan's version adds."}]}]},{"id":"lia-quick-write-explain","title":"Part C: Explain the Scene","minutes":6,"standards":["RL.6.4","RL.6.1","L.6.6"],"routine":"Quick Write","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Write 3-4 sentences answering: How does the battle at the Gateway Arch test Percy's courage when facing an ancient unknown? Cite at least one descriptive detail about the setting or the Chimera, and explain how one figurative phrase shapes the tone. Use at least two vocabulary words."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"Start with your claim. Then add evidence, then explain. For example: Riordan puts the Chimera in a modern landmark, so Percy's courage is tested because ___. For example, the text describes ___. This word choice shows ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"What does Percy do that shows courage, even though the monster is ancient and unknown?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Percy stays and fights the vicious Chimera even though he has no idea how to beat it. His joke about the Arch being a huge shopping bag handle shows he is nervous, but he still acts. This shows that courage means doing the brave thing while you are scared."},{"type":"eld-panel","purpose":"Support students in writing a short analysis with evidence, present-tense verbs, and academic vocabulary.","sayAsk":"Invite students to rehearse aloud first. Frames: Percy's courage is tested when ___. The text describes ___, which shows ___. The phrase ___ creates a ___ tone because ___. Encourage students to use the vocabulary words confined, vicious, enraged, or plummeted accurately.","watchFor":"If students write only a summary, then prompt: Add a sentence that begins with This shows... If students use the wrong tense for analysis, then prompt: Change the verb to present tense: Percy faces, not faced. Success looks like a claim, a cited detail, and an explanation of the tone."},{"type":"support-table","rows":[{"situation":"Struggling with: Writing an evidence-based explanation","tryThis":"Provide a paragraph frame: In Chapter 13, Percy faces ___. The author describes ___. This word choice shows ___, which tests Percy's courage because ___."},{"situation":"Ready for extension: Writing an evidence-based explanation","tryThis":"Ask students to add a sentence explaining how the modern setting makes the unknown feel more threatening, and to use the word spectacle or prowess precisely."}]}]}]},{"kind":"look-back","title":"Look Back","purpose":"Students reflect on how citing descriptive language helps explain how a scene is set up, a skill they will use in the performance task.","activities":[{"id":"lookback-reflection","title":"Reflect on Setting and Word Choice","minutes":5,"standards":["RL.6.4","L.6.6"],"routine":"Reflection","blocks":[{"type":"teacher-script","move":"say","text":"In your Performance Task, Shared Stories, Shared Lessons, you will cite descriptive language to explain how a scene is set up. Today you did that with the Gateway Arch and the Chimera."},{"type":"directions","text":"Complete the sentences: Riordan modernizes the battle by ___. The phrase ___ makes the tone ___ because ___. One new word I can use now is ___, which means ___."},{"type":"teacher-script","move":"ask","text":"Which of today's words will you use most when you explain a scene, and why?"},{"type":"sample-response","text":"Riordan modernizes the battle by putting the Chimera at the Gateway Arch, a real place people visit. The phrase huge shopping bag handle makes the tone funny because it compares a famous landmark to an everyday object. One new word I can use now is plummeted, which means fell straight down fast."}]}]},{"kind":"homework","title":"Homework (Optional)","purpose":"Students read Chapter 14 independently and annotate details that prepare them for the next Lesson.","activities":[{"id":"homework-read-ch14","title":"Read and Annotate Chapter 14","minutes":0,"standards":["RL.6.1"],"routine":"Annotation","blocks":[{"type":"directions","text":"Read *The Lightning Thief*, Chapter 14. As you read, annotate for details that show something unusual about what happens to Percy after the fall, and mark any word or phrase that creates a strong feeling. Bring your notes to the next class."}]}]}]},"digest":{"summary":"Students analyze the Chapter 13 battle at the Gateway Arch to explain how Riordan modernizes a classic hero-versus-monster fight through setting and Chimera details, and how figurative language such as the \"huge shopping bag handle\" shapes a humorous, high-stakes tone. They also use context clues and word parts to learn eight vocabulary words and record them in their Unit Vocabulary organizers.","keyActivities":["Context clues for confined, vicious, faithless, plummeted","Phonics and organizer: long i, -ous and -less","Annotating modern setting and Chimera details","Think-Pair-Share on the shopping bag handle comparison and tone","Quick Write explaining how the battle tests Percy's courage"],"vocabularyTaught":["confined","vicious","faithless","plummeted","modernize","prowess","enraged","spectacle"],"standardsCovered":["RL.6.4","L.6.4.a","RL.6.1","RL.6.6","L.6.6","ELD.PI.6.7","ELD.PI.6.6","ELD.PII.6.3"]}}
